config.title: Build typed command history undo redo

intro.title: Build typed command history undo redo
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a typed command history system that supports undo and redo operations. You will learn how to manage state changes in a type-safe way using TypeScript. The core concept involves implementing a command pattern with arrays to track history and a pointer for navigation. You'll use TypeScript interfaces, generics, and array methods to ensure your commands are strongly typed and reversible. By the end, you'll have a reusable module that can track, undo, and redo user actions safely.
intro.usecase: The command pattern with undo/redo functionality is essential in professional applications where users need to reverse or replay actions. You'll find this in design tools like Figma or Photoshop where every brush stroke or layer adjustment can be undone, in code editors like VS Code that track file changes, and in form-heavy applications like CRM systems where sales representatives might need to revert accidental data entries. As a developer, implementing typed command history ensures users can confidently interact with your application knowing they can recover from mistakes while you maintain type safety across all operations.

objectives: Implement a typed command interface to define undoable operations
Construct a command history manager to track executed commands
Manipulate the command stack to support undo and redo operations
Initialize application state with typed command history functionality
Apply command pattern principles to create reversible user actions
Configure undo/redo boundaries to prevent invalid state transitions
Update UI components to reflect current command history position

steps.title: Import TypeScript types and React hooks
steps.instruction: Import React, useState, and useRef from 'react'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in the necessary modules for your React component.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and hooks
import React, { useState, useRef } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React, useState, and useRef from 'react'
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports for React and the required hooks are added to the file.
successCriteria: React, useState, and useRef are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to import all three: React, useState, and useRef from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are not correct. You need to import React, useState, and useRef from 'react'.

steps.title: Define Command interface
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript interface named 'Command' with three properties: 'id' (string), 'name' (string), and 'timestamp' (Date).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with type annotations.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState, useRef } from 'react';
// Create the Command interface here
steps.expectedOutcome: A Command interface is defined with the correct property types, establishing the shape for command objects in your history system.
successCriteria: The Command interface exists with id: string, name: string, and timestamp: Date properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that all three properties (id, name, timestamp) are included with the correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Command interface isn't defined correctly. Make sure to use the 'interface' keyword and include all required properties with proper TypeScript types.

steps.title: Create main component with TypeScript
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named CommandHistory that returns null for now.
steps.hint: Use either function CommandHistory() { return null; } or const CommandHistory = () => null;
steps.expectedOutcome: A CommandHistory component is defined with proper TypeScript function component syntax.
successCriteria: The component is named CommandHistory and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the component is named exactly CommandHistory and returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check the name and return value.

steps.title: Initialize command history state
steps.instruction: Inside your CommandHistory component, initialize a state variable named 'commands' with useState. Set its initial value to an empty array and explicitly type it as Command[].
steps.hint: Use useState<Command[]>([]) to create a typed state variable for storing command history.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: typed array state
const [items, setItems] = useState<Item[]>([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a typed state variable 'commands' initialized to an empty array of Command objects.
successCriteria: The commands state is declared with useState<Command[]>([]) inside the component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure to use useState<Command[]>([]) with the correct type annotation.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're using useState with the Command[] type and an empty array initial value.

steps.title: Initialize current index state
steps.instruction: Inside the CommandHistory component, declare a state variable named 'currentIndex' with the number type and initialize it to -1.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with a type annotation to define the state variable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: typed state initialization
const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a typed state variable 'currentIndex' that tracks the current position in the command history.
successCriteria: The state variable 'currentIndex' is declared with the number type and initialized to -1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added state, but check that 'currentIndex' has the number type and is initialized to -1.
steps.feedbackWrong: The current index state is missing or incorrect. Declare a state variable named 'currentIndex' with type number and initial value -1.

steps.title: Create addCommand handler
steps.instruction: Inside the CommandHistory component, create a function named addCommand that takes a commandName parameter of type string and adds a new Command object to the commandHistory state array.
steps.hint: Define the function with proper TypeScript typing for the parameter. The function should create a new Command object with the provided name and add it to the history.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a typed addCommand function that can be used to add new commands to the history.
successCriteria: The addCommand function is defined with a string parameter, creates a Command object, and updates the commandHistory state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function properly creates a Command object and updates the state array.
steps.feedbackWrong: The addCommand function should take a string parameter and add a new Command object to the commandHistory state.

steps.title: Create redo handler
steps.instruction: Create a function called 'redo' inside your component that increments the currentIndex state when possible, with proper bounds checking.
steps.hint: The redo function should check if currentIndex is less than the last index of the commandHistory array before incrementing it.
steps.expectedOutcome: A typed redo function that safely increments the current index within array bounds.
successCriteria: The redo function is defined, checks bounds, and increments currentIndex appropriately.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the redo function, but ensure it properly checks if currentIndex is less than the last valid index before incrementing.
steps.feedbackWrong: The redo function is missing or doesn't correctly implement bounds checking. Review how to safely increment currentIndex within the commandHistory array length.

steps.title: Add command input structure
steps.instruction: Inside the CommandHistory component's return statement, add an input field with type 'text' and a button with text 'Add Command'.
steps.hint: Add the input and button JSX elements directly in the return statement. Use <input type="text" /> for the input and <button>Add Command</button> for the button.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will render a text input field and a button labeled 'Add Command'.
successCriteria: The return statement contains an input element with type='text' and a button element with the text 'Add Command'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have both an input field with type='text' and a button with the text 'Add Command'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input field or button is missing or incorrect. Add both elements as described.

steps.title: Add undo and redo buttons
steps.instruction: Add two buttons after the 'Add Command' button: one labeled 'Undo' and one labeled 'Redo'. Wire their onClick handlers to the undo and redo functions you created earlier.
steps.hint: Place the buttons inside the same div as the input and existing button. Use the handler names you defined in previous steps.
steps.expectedOutcome: Two new buttons appear in the UI after the 'Add Command' button, with proper labels and click handlers connected to the undo and redo functionality.
successCriteria: The UI contains an 'Undo' button with onClick={undoHandler} and a 'Redo' button with onClick={redoHandler}, placed after the existing button.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added the buttons, but check that both have correct onClick handlers pointing to your undo and redo functions.
steps.feedbackWrong: The undo and redo buttons are missing or incorrectly implemented. Make sure to add both buttons with proper labels and onClick handlers.

steps.title: Display current command
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element below the buttons to display the current command using optional chaining with the commands array and currentIndex.
steps.hint: Use commands[currentIndex]?.description to safely access the current command's description.
steps.expectedOutcome: A paragraph will appear below the buttons showing the description of the currently selected command, or nothing if no command exists at the current index.
successCriteria: A paragraph element is added that displays commands[currentIndex]?.description using optional chaining.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a paragraph, but make sure it uses optional chaining (commands[currentIndex]?.description) to safely access the current command.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph element is missing or doesn't correctly display the current command using optional chaining.

steps.title: Display full command history
steps.instruction: Below the current command display, add a list that maps through the command history array and renders each command with its index. Highlight the command at the current index with a different background color.
steps.hint: Use the map method on the command history state array. For each command, return a list item (<li>) containing the command text. Apply conditional styling to highlight the item when its index matches the current index state.
steps.expectedOutcome: A complete command history list appears below the current command display, with the command at the current index visually highlighted.
successCriteria: The component renders an unordered list (<ul>) that maps through the command history array, displays each command in a list item (<li>), and applies conditional styling to highlight the item at the current index.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added the list structure, but make sure to include the conditional styling to highlight the command at the current index.
steps.feedbackWrong: The command history list is not displaying correctly. Check that you're mapping through the command history array and applying the conditional styling based on the current index.
